the skin penetration of sunscreen ingredients and their metabolites is dependent on the chemical structure, and that this penetration is increased in the case of tyrosinase inhibiting sunscreens.

the use of human skin models to investigate the metabolism of cosmetic ingredients.
the development of novel in vitro models of the human skin, which are able to mimic the skin physiology and pathology.
the development of new methods and models for the in vitro testing of the effects of cosmetic ingredients, with the ultimate goal of improving the safety of cosmetic products.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no conclusive evidence that the use of sunscreens containing UV filters or tyrosinase inhibitor in cosmetics is increasing UV carcinogenicity in humans.
the use of tyrosinase inhibiting agents in sunscreens and cosmetic formulations does not increase UV carcinogenicity.
the use of tyrosinase inhibitor in sunscreens and/or cosmetics is not a risk factor for the development of skin cancer.

the in vitro models of EHS and EKS are suitable tools to investigate the effects of cosmetic ingredients, and to predict the skin penetration and metabolism of the ingredients.

the in vitro skin models are useful for studying the effects of UV radiation on the skin, but they cannot fully mimic the in vivo conditions, as the skin models lack the vascularization, the dermis, and the epidermal turnover.
